title: 3-Read Friday #97: Cognitive Offloading, LLM Tutors, and Mini Whiteboards
author: Craig Barton
summary: In 3-Read Friday #97, Barton curates three posts spanning AI use, tutoring, and classroom tools. Paul Kirschner corrects a common terminology error, arguing that what students and teachers do when they hand a complex task to AI without engaging their own thinking is better described as cognitive outsourcing rather than cognitive offloading, and that the distinction has real implications for how we understand the risk. Daisy Christodoulou examines an Eedi-and-Google study on whether large language model tutors can work, giving a largely positive verdict while raising genuine challenges. Dylan Kane returns to a classroom staple, mini whiteboards, walking through exactly what he uses them for and how he makes the routine work day to day. Barton's own framing ties the AI-focused pieces to a broader theme of being precise about what AI tools actually do to student thinking.
points: Kirschner's terminology correction matters practically: 'cognitive offloading' describes shifting a memory or processing burden onto a tool, while handing the entire thinking task to AI without engagement is 'outsourcing' -- a distinct and more concerning failure mode.
Christodoulou's read of the Eedi/Google LLM-tutor study is cautiously positive but not uncritical -- it identifies real challenges alongside genuine promise, avoiding both hype and dismissal.
Kane's mini-whiteboard post is a reminder that durable low-tech routines still repay careful, explicit articulation of exactly what they're for and how to run them well.
Barton's own vested interest (Eedi ran the study Christodoulou reviews) is disclosed transparently, modelling how to handle conflict-of-interest in curation.
quotes: I have definitely used the phrase "cognitive offloading" to describe what students (or teachers!) do when they give a complex task to AI and do not engage in the thinking themselves.
It turns out that is not the phrase I should be using, and the distinction matters!
Warning: I have more than a vested interest in this post by Daisy, as it discusses a study my company, Eedi, did with Google.
It was fascinating to get Daisy's take on it, which was largely positive, and also consider her challenges.
It's been a while (too long?) since we had a mini-whiteboard post, so here you go. Dylan takes a deep dive into exactly what he uses mini-whiteboards for and how he makes it work.
